summary: Describes 6to4 Provider Managed Tunnels, a framework operators can use to manage 6to4 tunnels in an anycast setup and improve the experience when the network is performing poorly or breaking. It is now historic and was replaced by RFC 7526.

eli5.summary: A shortcut tunnel to the IPv6 world sometimes got blocked or slow. This memo had a way for the tunnel owners to help keep it working. It is now historic.

subtitle: A way to fix broken IPv6 tunnels in systems running on shared IPv4 addresses.

tldr.problem: 6to4 tunnels automatically set up IPv6 connectivity but fail or perform poorly when endpoints are behind Carrier-Grade NAT (CGN), especially with non-RFC1918 IPv4 addresses, leaving the return path broken.
tldr.mechanism: 6to4 Provider Managed Tunnels (6to4-PMT) intercept 6to4 traffic at a provider relay and translate the IPv6 source prefix from the standard 6to4 prefix to a provider-assigned prefix, restoring control over the forwarding path.
tldr.outcome: This gives operators a simple way to fix broken 6to4 operation while native IPv6 deployment is underway, and systems with native IPv6 available will prefer that instead. RFC 7526 provides a later update.

today: RFC 6732 is Historic and has been superseded by RFC 7526. 6to4-PMT was a working interim solution for operators deploying IPv6 before native IPv6 was widely available. Modern deployments use native dual-stack or newer transition technologies.

sections.title: Introduction and Motivation
sections.content:
RFC 6732 introduces 6to4 Provider Managed Tunnels (6to4-PMT), a framework to manage 6to4 tunnels when they operate in anycast mode (where clients automatically discover a relay with no explicit configuration). Anycast-based 6to4, defined in RFC 3068, is built into many operating systems and home gateways but has a critical weakness: the return path is uncontrolled and can be high-latency or broken entirely.

The problem is especially acute in networks using Carrier-Grade NAT (CGN) [RFC 6264]. When a device behind CGN is assigned a non-RFC1918 IPv4 address (such as shared address space [RFC 6598]), the device may auto-enable 6to4, but the return path from the IPv6 Internet will be routed to an address not owned by the local network, breaking the connection. Operators deploying IPv6 need an interim solution while native IPv6 is still unavailable; 6to4-PMT offers one.
sections.eli5: Lots of devices had 6to4 turned on by default, but it broke when those devices shared an address or were behind a NAT. Operators needed a quick fix.

sections.title: The 6to4-PMT Model
sections.content:
6to4-PMT operates in two stages: the customer's IPv6-capable device sends 6to4-encapsulated traffic to a local relay (just as standard 6to4 does), but the 6to4-PMT relay adds a prefix translation function. It decapsulates the IPv6 packet, translates the source IPv6 address from the standard 6to4 prefix (2002::/16) to a provider-assigned prefix (for example, 2001:db8::/32), re-encapsulates it, and sends it onward to the IPv6 Internet.

The function can be deployed stateless (with deterministic prefix mappings that require no state) or stateful. In stateless mode, the operator can place multiple relays in the network without managing shared translation state, and customers can receive inbound services using the translated prefix. The translated address is routable under the operator's peering, making the path predictable and controllable by normal IPv6 routing policy.
sections.eli5: The relay swaps the IPv6 address label before forwarding the packet onward, so return traffic comes back to the right place.

sections.title: Deployment Considerations
sections.content:
6to4-PMT relays should allow customers to opt out, though an opt-out strategy is more practical for non-technical users than opt-in, since most devices have 6to4 enabled by default and users are generally unaware of it. The relay should advertise the well-known 6to4 anycast range (192.88.99.0/24) in the provider's local IPv4 network to attract 6to4 traffic, and optionally filter that range from customer-originated advertisements to ensure all 6to4 traffic stays local.

Implementations must handle Path MTU Discovery correctly: the 6to4 tunnel reduces the effective MTU, and the relay should send ICMP Packet Too Big messages using the translated address. Checksum updates depend on whether the translation is stateless or stateful. The relay can be deployed on existing 6to4 infrastructure or on standalone platforms; vendors have already shipped implementations.
sections.eli5: Operators need to turn this on in their network, let customers turn it off if they want, and make sure packet sizes and checksums still work.

sections.title: Status and Use
sections.content:
RFC 6732 is an Informational document, not a standards-track specification. It describes a technique that has been successfully deployed in production networks, with open-source implementations and at least one major router vendor's implementation. However, 6to4-PMT is explicitly intended as an interim measure.

Once native IPv6 becomes available to a customer endpoint, the device will prefer native IPv6 over 6to4 via correct address selection [RFC 6724], and 6to4-PMT is no longer needed. The RFC was marked Historic in 2018 and superseded by RFC 7526, which carries the same concept forward.
sections.eli5: This was a working stopgap while operators rolled out real IPv6. Once native IPv6 arrived, devices would pick that instead.
